title: They Got Paid $12,000 to Move to West Virginia — and They're Staying!
summary: Have you ever dreamed of packing up and moving to a new place — and getting paid to do it? That's exactly what happened to Ashley Eklin. In 2022, she was living in Chicago when she found out about a program called Ascend West Virginia. The deal? Move to West Virginia, and they'd give her $12,000 over two years! Ashley had never even visited the state before. "I literally had never been to West Virginia. I hadn't even visited, and I bought a house," she says. Now she lives in Inwood, a small town with just 3,400 people. She spends her free time kayaking, hiking, and taking photos of the stars — something she couldn't do in the bright lights of Chicago. Ascend West Virginia started in 2021, right when many people began working from home because of the pandemic. The program was created by Brad D. Smith, a former CEO who grew up in West Virginia. He wanted to help his home state, which has been losing people for decades. In fact, West Virginia is the only state with fewer people today than in 1950! The program is paid for by a private foundation, not taxes. So far, it's been so popular that they've started new versions: one for teachers, one for veterans, and one to keep college graduates from leaving. Abby Snyder and her husband Colin Scott were digital nomads — people who work online while traveling the world. They were living in Portugal when they heard about Ascend West Virginia. They decided to move to Lewisburg and are now putting down roots. "We need to be part of this fight for our democracy," Abby says. It turns out that sometimes, a little cash and a lot of natural beauty can make a place feel like home.
why_it_matters: You might discover that some places are so eager for new neighbors that they'll pay families to move there, which could affect where your own family might choose to live one day.

background_read: Some towns and states offer cash to attract new residents, like Tulsa, Oklahoma, which has a similar program for remote workers.
West Virginia has been losing population for many years because of fewer coal mining jobs.
Brad D. Smith (the former CEO who founded Ascend West Virginia) hoped to reverse this trend by bringing in people who work from home.
Article_Structure: WHO: Ashley Eklin, Abby Snyder, Colin Scott, and others who moved to West Virginia.
WHAT: They received $12,000 over two years to relocate to small towns like Inwood and Lewisburg.
WHERE: West Virginia, a state with fewer people now than in 1950.
WHY: To reverse the state's long-term population loss and attract new residents, especially with more remote work.
